title: What Is the Tooth Pulp, and Why Does It Get Infected?
metaTitle: What Is Tooth Pulp and Why It Gets Infected
metaDescription: The tooth pulp is the living tissue inside your tooth. Learn what it does, how decay, cracks, and trauma infect it, and why removing it can save the tooth.
excerpt: The pulp is the nerve and blood supply inside your tooth. Here is what it does, how decay, cracks, and trauma let bacteria infect it, and why removing it saves the tooth.
heroImageAlt: A cross-section diagram of a tooth showing enamel, dentin, and the inner pulp chamber.
bodyHtml:
The tooth pulp is the soft living tissue at the centre of your tooth, made up of nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue that nourish the tooth and let it sense temperature and pressure. It becomes infected when bacteria reach it, usually through deep decay, a crack, a leaking filling, or an injury. Once bacteria get into this normally sealed space, the pulp can inflame and then die, and the infection may spread toward the root tip. Understanding what the pulp is helps explain why a root canal, which removes that infected tissue, can save a tooth rather than lose it.

A quick tour of tooth anatomy

A tooth has a few main layers. The hard outer enamel is the white surface you see. Beneath it lies dentin, a slightly softer layer that makes up most of the tooth. At the core is the pulp chamber, which extends down through narrow channels called root canals into the roots that anchor the tooth in the jaw. The pulp runs through this inner space, connecting to the body through tiny openings at the root tips.

In a healthy, developing tooth, the pulp supplies nutrients and helps form dentin. In an adult tooth, the pulp is less essential for day-to-day function, which is why a tooth can survive and work normally after the pulp is removed during a root canal.

What the pulp does

The pulp has two main jobs. First, its blood vessels nourish the tooth while it develops and keep the inner tissue alive. Second, its nerves provide sensation, including that sharp message you get from something very hot, cold, or sweet. This is why a tooth with inflamed pulp can be so sensitive: the nerves are reacting to irritation.

How the pulp becomes infected

The pulp is normally protected by enamel and dentin. Infection happens when that protection is breached and bacteria find a path inside:

Deep decay. A cavity left untreated can burrow through enamel and dentin until it reaches the pulp, carrying bacteria with it.

Cracks and chips. A crack can open a channel straight to the pulp, even if the break looks minor on the surface.

Repeated dental work. Large or repeated fillings on the same tooth can stress the pulp over time, and a leaking restoration can let bacteria seep underneath.

Trauma. A knock to a tooth can damage the pulp or its blood supply, sometimes causing it to die slowly, even years later and without pain.

Why removing infected pulp saves the tooth

Once the pulp is infected, it does not heal on its own, and the infection tends to progress toward the bone around the root. A root canal removes the infected pulp, disinfects the inside of the tooth, and seals it, stopping the infection while keeping the natural tooth structure in place. Because an adult tooth does not depend on the pulp to function, it can continue to bite and chew normally afterward, usually protected by a filling or crown.

If the pulp is removed, is the tooth dead?

People sometimes call a treated tooth "dead" because it no longer has a living nerve, but the tooth remains firmly in place and fully functional. It is supported by the surrounding bone and ligament, which keep it stable.

Will I still feel hot and cold afterward?

The treated tooth itself will no longer sense temperature, since its nerve has been removed. Your other teeth continue to feel normally, and most people do not notice the difference in everyday eating.

Can an infected pulp be prevented?

Often, yes. Treating cavities early, protecting teeth from cracks, and keeping up regular checkups can catch problems before they reach the pulp. Good daily care goes a long way toward keeping that inner tissue healthy.

Knowing what the pulp is and how it gets infected can make a recommended root canal feel far more logical.
